It also shows how to use LaTeX formula - for that one usually needs
the assistence of a webserver - thus the root script via

system(command)

starts a local webserver.

Sources, comments and video are shown.

5. Tribute to John Conway: Game of Life in root

John Horton Conway FRS (26 December 1937 - 11 April 2020)
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Horton_Conway widely known for his Game of Life.
See the wikipedia description with animations!

The code is a rewrite of a simple matlab demo algorithm, but using
a simple terminal "typewriter art".

The program was made quickly for the exercise. Improve the code by
removing the unnecessary elements, like unused functions etc.
It is a good exercise on "cleaning the code".

The "mechanism" of screen graphics is demonstrated in updater.C

Task: simplify the program(s). See file README.txt
Try to understand the matlab method and its C++ implementation.


From wikipedia:
- Any live cell with two or three live neighbors survives.
- Any dead cell with three live neighbors becomes a live cell.
- All other live cells die in the next generation.
- Similarly, all other dead cells stay dead.

This can be implemented (where N is the number of living neighbors)

             X = (int)( ( X && (N==2) ) || N==3 );

saying X will live if it has just 2 alive neighbors or a cell will be(come) alive
if 3 neighbours are alive. If there are more neighbors, the cell will be 0, die,
because there is no N==4 in the assignment above.
Alive is 1, not alive/dead is 0     (int)false=0         (int)true =1

First of all, run and explore the codes included.
The most general one with random start is shown below.

Clean the code, the formatting got mixed up. Structure the for loops
nicely to show the logic of the code (especially the main loop up to Ncyc.)

7. Canvas Events - clicks, mouse move, keyboard

ROOT has naturally built in the possibility to register the user's actions on
the graphics, as we have seen in earlier exercises.

But how can you get access to these "events"? It is all that you can do as a user,
clicking in the TCanvas or hitting the keyboard keys, (right click is blocked?),
left click, moving the mouse with pressed button etc.

I have modified a tutorial example to print in the terminal all the events which
root sees - i.e. what I was able to find out. So you run the explore_events.C
and place the terminal so that you can see all the printing.

You will find below that the events are worked on in clicks_func.C
the relevant lines are repeated here:
          cout << event<< endl;
          int px = gPad->GetEventX(); // event data
          int py = gPad->GetEventY();
          cout << px << " " << py << endl;
So you see, it prints the event type (one number) and then the data.

file explore_events.C (and following clicks_func.C )
Is in the directory EVENTS
If you would program a game or a GUI based project
you could use such techniques.
Explore this and as a simple exercise try to add a line into the clicks_func.C (next listing)
which would EXIT ROOT when you hit a special keyboard key (e.g. q-letter)
( remember the gROOT->ProcessLine(".q") ?)
(on my Mac - I hope it is universal event==24 px==113 for q - and px==81 for Q)

 
clicks_func.C    - reaction to all EVENTS -     used by    explore_events.C
Note the line      c1->AddExec("ex","clicks_func()");      adds this as event handling function to TCanvas *c1
